kurz: How to weigh the tax deferral of a variable annuity against its annual costs and the higher tax rate at the end, and what cash-value life insurance adds to the picture.

bloecke.md:
A variable annuity is an insurance contract that holds investment subaccounts, often funds that are very similar to the index funds you could also buy yourself in a brokerage account. The investment can therefore be the same; the difference lies in the legal construction. The insurer owns the subaccounts, and you hold a contract with the insurer. All the other differences follow from this: the tax deferral, the tax-free switch between subaccounts, the option of lifetime income and the additional costs of the insurance contract.

Whether the annuity or the brokerage account comes out ahead can therefore be calculated. On one side is the deferral: in the annuity, dividends and interest are not taxed every year. On the other side are two disadvantages. One is a cost that acts every year on the *entire assets*. The other acts once, at the end, on the *gain*: the annuity's gain is taxed at ordinary income tax rates, not at the lower rates for long-term capital gains.

## Taxation of annuity and brokerage account

This lesson is about a *nonqualified* annuity, that is, one bought with money that has already been taxed, outside an IRA or a 401(k). Under 26 U.S.C. § 72, its earnings are not taxed until they are withdrawn. Withdrawals count as earnings first and only then as a return of the premiums paid in, and the earnings are taxed as ordinary income at your marginal tax rate. Before age 59½, an additional 10% tax applies to the taxable part (§ 72(q)), with a few exceptions. At death, the gain does not disappear: the heirs pay ordinary income tax on it.

In the brokerage account, the gain on shares held for more than one year is a long-term capital gain, taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% under § 1(h). For 2026, the 0% rate applies up to a taxable income of $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly; the 20% rate begins at $545,500 and $613,700. Qualified dividends are taxed at the same rates in the year they are paid. The 3.8% net investment income tax above a modified adjusted gross income of $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (joint) hits the gain in both wrappers and drops out of the comparison. At death, the cost basis of inherited shares is stepped up to the market value (§ 1014), so the gain accrued until then is never taxed as income. State income taxes come on top in most states and are left out here.

bloecke.md:
## Costs as the yardstick

The costs of a variable annuity are listed in the fee table of its prospectus. The largest item is usually the mortality and expense risk charge, which the SEC describes as typically around 1.25% a year. Administrative fees and the expenses of the subaccount funds come on top, and optional riders with guaranteed income or death benefits often cost another 1% a year or more. With commission-based contracts, the total therefore often lies between about 2% and 3% a year. That is a range from typical fee tables, not official statistics. A few providers sell contracts without commission and with total costs well below 1%. A broad index ETF in a brokerage account costs between about 0.03% and 0.10% a year.

This gap is considerable. It is a difference between two returns, and differences in return grow exponentially over the term, while the value of the deferral depends on how much tax would otherwise have been due along the way.

bloecke.titel: Illustrative calculation with $500 a month over 30 years at a 7% gross return before all costs
Final capital after 30 years, split into payout and tax (illustrative calculation)
bloecke.unter: With $180,000 paid in each case, the commission-based annuity leaves about $162,000 less than the brokerage account, and even the low-cost annuity is about $46,000 behind.

bloecke.md:
The calculation assumes a marginal tax rate of 22% and a capital gains rate of 15% in the years of withdrawal. The ETF pays 1.5% a year in qualified dividends, which are taxed at 15% every year; these taxes, around $13,000 over 30 years, have already been deducted from the brokerage value. A sale at the end is assumed for the brokerage account. The cost of 0.45% for the annuity without commission is an assumption for this calculation, as is the 2.25% for the commission-based contract (mortality and expense charge, administration and fund expenses, without riders). State taxes are not taken into account.

These simplifications do not change the ranking. Even the low-cost annuity loses, because the 7-point higher rate on the gain at the end weighs more than deferring the tax on a 1.5% dividend yield. Under these assumptions the annuity would still lose at zero cost: $498,300 net against $507,600. Broad equity index funds are already tax-efficient in a brokerage account, so there is little left for the annuity to defer.

## Break-even calculation

The deferral is worth more for assets whose income is taxed at ordinary rates every year, such as bond funds. In the brokerage account, their interest is taxed annually at the marginal rate; in the annuity, it is taxed only once, at the end, at the same rate. The reverse calculation determines the maximum annual cost an annuity holding a bond fund may have so that the end result equals that of the same fund in a brokerage account.

With $500 a month over 30 years, a bond fund yielding 4.5% and costs of 0.05% in the brokerage account, the limit is narrow. At a marginal tax rate of 12% the annuity may cost around 0.23% a year, at 22% around 0.37%, at 24% around 0.39% and at 32% around 0.50%. Depending on the tax rate, the deferral therefore offsets only about 0.2 to 0.45 percentage points of additional annual costs.

bloecke.unter: Calculated against the same bond fund at 0.05% in a brokerage account over 30 years; the reference line marks the typical mortality and expense charge alone, before fund expenses and riders.

bloecke.md: In a nonqualified annuity, you exchange the lower capital gains rate and the step-up in basis at death for tax deferral. For broad equity index funds this exchange almost never pays off. For bonds it only pays off if the contract costs little more than a fund. The fee table in the prospectus is the first thing to look for in an offer.

## Tax-advantaged accounts come first

The deferral that an annuity sells is available without insurance costs in the accounts that the tax code provides for retirement. In 2026 you can contribute up to $24,500 to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457(b) plan, plus a catch-up of $8,000 from age 50 and $11,250 at ages 60 to 63. The IRA limit is $7,500, plus $1,100 from age 50. Traditional accounts defer the tax; Roth accounts grow tax-free. A health savings account can be added if you have an eligible high-deductible health plan.

Buying an annuity *inside* an IRA or a 401(k) adds no further tax deferral, because the account is already tax-deferred; the SEC points this out explicitly. In this case, you only pay for the insurance features, and it is worth checking whether you actually need them.

## Switching and surrender

The second argument for the annuity is the tax-free switch between subaccounts, and it is valid. Reallocating or rebalancing within the contract does not trigger tax. In the brokerage account, every sale realizes gains. There, however, you can choose which tax lots to sell, rebalance with new contributions and dividends, and offset gains with realized losses. For a buy-and-hold investor with a single total-market fund, the tax-free switch is worth nothing, because it is an option that goes unused.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 1035, an annuity can be exchanged for another annuity without tax, and a life insurance policy for an annuity. This is the way out of an expensive contract, but the new contract may start a new surrender period. Exiting for cash is expensive. Most contracts charge a surrender fee in the first years; the SEC describes a typical schedule that starts around 7% and falls by one point a year. Many contracts allow you to withdraw about 10% a year without this fee. Before 59½, the additional 10% tax on the earnings portion applies on top.

bloecke.md:
## Annuitization and the exclusion ratio

If you convert the contract into lifelong payments instead of withdrawing it, the taxation changes. Under § 72(b), each payment is split by the *exclusion ratio* into a tax-free return of the premiums paid in and taxable earnings. The ratio is the investment in the contract divided by the expected return, which the IRS calculates with the life expectancy multiples in Publication 939. Example: $180,000 paid in, $1,500 a month for life from age 65, and a multiple of 20.0 years for a 65-year-old in Table V. The expected return is $360,000, so 50% of every payment is tax-free until the $180,000 have been recovered; after that, payments are fully taxable. If you die before then, the unrecovered amount can be deducted on the final tax return.

The amount of the payments depends on the annuity rates. Contracts contain guaranteed annuitization rates, which are calculated very cautiously. At annuitization, insurers usually apply their current rates if these are higher. Only the guaranteed rates are binding when you sign.

bloecke.titel: The benefit base is not money
bloecke.md: Riders with guaranteed lifetime withdrawals advertise a yearly “roll-up” of, say, 5% on the benefit base. That figure is not a return. The benefit base is only a number from which the guaranteed annual withdrawal is calculated. It cannot be withdrawn as a lump sum. With a benefit base of $300,000 and a withdrawal percentage of 5%, the rider pays $15,000 a year for life, even if the actual account value is only $220,000. What you or your heirs can really get is the account value, and it grows only with the subaccounts after all fees, including the rider fee. If a contract is bought for the guarantee, compare the guaranteed lifetime payment with the price of a plain income annuity, not the roll-up with a market return.

## Cash-value life insurance

Whole life, universal life and indexed universal life policies combine a death benefit with a savings component, the cash value. In tax terms they are attractive: the cash value grows tax-deferred, the death benefit is generally free of income tax (§ 101(a)), and loans against the policy are not taxed as long as the policy stays in force. If a policy is funded faster than the limits of § 7702A allow, it becomes a modified endowment contract; loans and withdrawals are then taxed like an annuity, earnings first and with the additional 10% tax before 59½. If a policy lapses with a loan outstanding, the gain becomes taxable at once.

The costs work against this. The cost of insurance, administration charges and commissions are concentrated in the first years, so the [[Surrender value|surrender value]] is usually far below the premiums paid for a long time. Anyone who needs life insurance to replace income while children are young usually covers this more cheaply with term insurance and invests the difference. Permanent insurance can be justified where the need itself is lifelong, for example to provide liquidity for an estate or for a dependent who will always need support.

bloecke.titel: Cases in favour of the annuity
bloecke.md:
In some situations, the annuity can come out ahead:

- You already contribute the maximum to all tax-advantaged accounts, you are in a high bracket today, you want to hold bonds or other tax-inefficient assets for decades, and you can buy a contract without commission at a cost close to that of a fund.
- The goal is longevity protection rather than return. What counts then is the guaranteed lifelong payment. It is an insurance benefit that protects against a very long life and is paid for with return. Plain income annuities, covered in a later lesson, usually deliver this more cheaply than riders on a variable annuity.
- In some states, annuities and life insurance enjoy stronger protection from creditors than a brokerage account. The rules differ considerably from state to state.

In all other cases, at today's usual cost levels, the brokerage account comes out better.

The calculation above applies to a new contract. With an existing contract, the commission has already been paid and cannot be recovered. In the comparison with the brokerage account, only the future costs then count, together with the surrender charge still due and, before 59½, the additional 10% tax. A § 1035 exchange into a low-cost annuity avoids immediate tax on the gain and is often better than cashing out. Older contracts can contain valuable guarantees, such as high guaranteed annuitization rates or a rider whose benefit base is far above the account value. Such a guarantee should be valued before it is given up.

mitnehmen: Because the annuity's costs act every year on the entire assets and its gain is taxed at ordinary rates, the deferral rarely makes up for the disadvantages.

In a brokerage account, long-term gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, and heirs receive a step-up in basis; in a nonqualified annuity, the gain is taxed as ordinary income, also for the heirs.

For an equity index fund, the annuity loses even at zero cost in the illustrative calculation; for a bond fund, the deferral offsets only about 0.2 to 0.45 percentage points of additional annual costs.
401(k), IRA and HSA provide deferral without insurance costs, and an annuity inside them adds no further tax advantage.
For annuitization and riders, only guaranteed figures count; a roll-up on the benefit base is not a return.

begriffe.text: Insurance contract whose value depends on investment subaccounts chosen by the owner. Earnings are tax-deferred until withdrawal and then taxed as ordinary income. The contract charges insurance and administration fees in addition to the fund expenses.
Annuity bought with money that has already been taxed, outside an IRA or employer plan. The premiums paid in come back tax-free as basis; only the earnings are taxable.

Share of each annuity payment that is treated as a tax-free return of the investment in the contract under 26 U.S.C. § 72(b). It equals the investment divided by the expected return and applies until the investment has been recovered.

Annual fee of a variable annuity that pays for the insurance guarantees and part of the insurer's costs and commissions. According to the SEC, it is typically around 1.25% of the account value a year.

Tax-free exchange of one annuity for another, or of a life insurance policy for an annuity or another life insurance policy, under 26 U.S.C. § 1035. The gain is carried over and taxed only on later withdrawals.
Fee that an insurer deducts if money is withdrawn from an annuity during the first years beyond the free amount. It usually declines year by year until it disappears.
